references.text: The Israelites expressed similar concerns about food in the wilderness and asked what they should eat, showing humanity's tendency to doubt God's provision.
God tested the Israelites with manna to teach them that people do not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the Lord's mouth—a lesson on trusting in God's provision.
This is God's direct answer to the question in verse 20, where he promises to send his blessing in the sixth year so that the harvest will last for three years.
Jesus teaches not to worry about food and drink but to seek first God's kingdom and trust that the Father will provide—the same principle of trusting in God's provision.
Jesus warns against asking 'What shall we eat?' as the Gentiles do, pointing out that the heavenly Father knows what we need.
Paul assures that God will supply all their needs according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus, confirming the principle of divine provision.
God promised to provide for Elijah at the brook Cherith with water and food from ravens, as an example of his supernatural provision when human resources are lacking.
David testifies that he has never seen the righteous forsaken or their children begging for bread, confirming God's faithful provision.
